15 proven decision-making principles:
I wish I knew these at age 25.
(These help avoid most bad decisions)

1️⃣ Newspaper Test
↳ Make decisions you'd feel good about if the whole world found out.

2️⃣ Sunk Cost
↳ Ignore past investments when deciding what creates the best future.

3️⃣ Availability Heuristic
↳ Don’t confuse what comes to mind easily with what’s most likely.

4️⃣ Stoic Dichotomy
↳ Focus your energy only on what you can control.

5️⃣ Average Payoff
↳ Choose based on the average long-term payoff, not the most likely outcome.

6️⃣ Categorical Imperative
↳ Only follow principles you’d be comfortable with everyone following.

7️⃣ Know Thyself
↳ Good decisions begin with self-awareness.

8️⃣ Golden Rule
↳ Treat others the way you’d want to be treated.

9️⃣ Fair Play
↳ Don’t go against the grain until you can clearly explain why others are wrong.

1️⃣0️⃣ Lindy Effect
↳ The longer an idea has survived, the longer it’s likely to keep surviving.

1️⃣1️⃣ Middle Way
↳ Avoid destructive extremes and choose the balanced path.

1️⃣2️⃣ First-Idea Bias
↳ Don’t give the first idea you hear undue weight.

1️⃣3️⃣ Confirmation Bias
↳ Seek evidence that could prove you wrong before you decide.

1️⃣4️⃣ Comparative Advantage
↳ Ask yourself: Where do I have a natural advantage?

1️⃣5️⃣ Age 80 + age 10 Test
↳ Make choices your younger and older selves would both admire.

90% of decisions can be solved with these 15 ideas.

I’ve worked with seven top 0.1% creators this year. Most are wrestling with the same problem. Here’s how to overcome it.

Most LinkedIn creators go through 5 phases.
This is why they rise. And eventually fall.
Here’s how to avoid the trap:

1️⃣ Phase 1: Early Struggle

At this point, nothing is working.
So the creator is willing to try everything.

And they typically do.

Copying other people’s posts, comment tactics, wild DM strategies, AI writing, human writing, lead magnets, engagement pods, courses, coaches and even buying followers.

Nothing works until...

2️⃣ Phase 2: Moment of Inspiration

The creator finds a golden tool. Maybe even two.
That golden tool leads to audience growth.
And often their first leads or clients.

It might be:

→ A certain post format
→ A writing style
→ A hook structure
→ A visual aesthetic
→ A trend
→ A content type

The creator believes they’ve unlocked the secrets of the universe.

Which leads to...

3️⃣ Phase 3: Systematizing

The creator builds systems to make that golden tool work more efficiently.

This is where they create:

→ A content calendar
→ Content pillars
→ AI prompts
→ Hook generators
→ Repeatable post structures
→ Automations

The creator leans back in their chair, ready to ride their system off into the sunset.

Until...

4️⃣ Phase 4: Stagnation

The system stops working.
The golden tool has turned into cardboard.
Impressions, followers and leads slow down.

But rather than going back to phases 1 and 2...

Which is what would keep the brand alive!!!!

The creator doubles down on the system.

“I just need to make my hooks tighter.”
“I just need to stick closer to my pillars.”
“I just need MORE AI help.”

But it never works.
Because the platform has evolved.

And NO golden tool lasts forever.
No matter how well it worked six months ago.

5️⃣ Phase 5: Departure

The creator tries TikTok, Instagram and Substack.
Then eventually gives up and gets a real job.

So...

If things are slowing down for you, but you’re still using the same strategy you used six months ago...

Don’t blame the algo.
And don't blame AI saturation.

It would be nice to build a system that worked forever.
But that is just not how life or social media works.

Become a beginner again.
Keep experimenting.
Until you find your next golden tool.

But next time, don't get hooked on it.
Use it until it stops working.
Then experiment again.

You got this.

It’s the same journey from startup freedom to enterprise ick.

You don’t need to treat yourself with the same bureaucracy and constraints as a massive company.

You are a creator.

Stay in startup mode.

11 life principles I wish knew 20 years ago:
(These solve nearly work related problems)

1️⃣ Hofstadter’s Law
↳ Everything takes longer than you expect. Even when you expect it to.

2️⃣ Chesterton’s Fence
↳ Before changing something, understand why it exists in the first place.

3️⃣ Hanlon’s Razor
↳ Don’t assume someone is malicious when carelessness explains it just fine.

4️⃣ Parkinson’s Law
↳ Work expands to fill the time you give it. Shorter deadlines create faster action.

5️⃣ Brooks’s Law
↳ Adding more people to a late project often makes it even later.

6️⃣ Goodhart’s Law
↳ Once a metric becomes the goal, people start gaming the metric.

7️⃣ Occam’s Razor
↳ When two explanations fit the facts, the simpler one is usually the better place to start.

8️⃣ Hick’s Law
↳ More choices create slower decisions. Simplify your options to move faster.

9️⃣ The Pareto Principle
↳ A small percentage of your actions usually creates most of your results.

🔟 The Dunning–Kruger Effect
↳ The less skilled you are, the harder it can be to recognize how much you still don’t know.

1️⃣1️⃣ The Peter Principle
↳ People often keep getting promoted until they reach a job they’re bad at.

90% of my day-to-day work issues could’ve been solved by one of these.

→ Relatable stories
→ Shared frustrations

When it comes to this kind of virality, 100% agree.

2️⃣ Debate Virality

This is the loudest kind of viral.

What is debate virality?
→ Strong POVs
→ Hot takes
→ Black-and-white framing
→ Content people argue about

How can you tell you hit debate virality?
↳ Likes: ~2–3% of impressions
↳ Comments: 0.6–1.5%
↳ Saves: 0.3–0.8%

This can be good or bad for your business
→ Massive visibility
→ Strong POV positioning

What is resource virality?
→ Tactical frameworks
→ Repeatable systems

Content people actually save.

1️⃣ The problem is known and specific

2️⃣ The problem is urgent

Time, money, or personal satisfaction on the line.

3️⃣ The outcome is narrow

More accessible and, therefore, more exciting.

7️⃣ The commitment is short-term

This was the hardest part about selling conference talk prep.

It's a TON of work for the buyer.

If you're asking to fundamentally alter someone's business or department, it will be harder to sell...

Average thinkers often nail it. Why?

How to build an audience on LI is a bit misleading.

You might think it's about...

→ the quality of your thinking
→ the strength of your product
→ your years of experience

But it has little to do with that.

It actually depends on where you create on the spectrum.

Here’s what I mean (and how people get this wrong):

Content exists on a spectrum.

→ On one end it's tactical & action-oriented
→ On the other it's high-level & outcome-oriented
→ And everything in between

Roughly 6 layers total.

Here’s what it looks like at a glance.

Detailed / Practical
↑
 | Layer 1 — Tactical help
 | Layer 2 — Guides & walkthroughs
 | Layer 3 — Framework content
 | Layer 4 — Strategy-level content
 | Layer 5 — Your point of view
 | Layer 6 — The outcomes you provide
↓
High Level / Abstract

Here’s what happens when you roll the content out:

→ The outer layers attract practitioners.
→ The inner layers attract stakeholders.

→ The inner layers can help close deals.
→ The outer layers are what grow your audience.

Here’s the problem for smart people:

Brilliant people often prefer layers 4, 5 & 6.

→ They think that anything else is "dumbing it down."
→ So they focus there... and their reach stays tiny.

Average thinkers often prefer layers 1, 2 & 3.

→ It feels fun and intuitive to them.
→ So they focus there... and their audience grows.

Yes, you need all 6 layers for a long-term business.

But it's generally best to build from the outside in.

→ Focus on the outer layers
→ Build an audience by helping people win
→ Then move inward as you grow

There’s a lot of debate on this.

"You don't need to have a big following!"
"Just reach the RIGHT people."

There’s some truth to that.

But think about it this way:

You can sell to people who barely know you.
|
or
|
You can sell to people who already follow you.

I recommend the second option.

"How do I find the right design for my infographic?"
Here are 8 core layouts to choose from: ↓↓↓

Turns out there's only 8 core visual layouts.
After making hundreds that's what I've found.

That's good news for two reasons.

1) It simplifies your choices
2) Almost every idea can fit any of them

It's just a matter of seeing which one feels best for the nuance you're trying to get across.

Here's the quick breakdown of when to use all 8.

1️⃣ The Venn Diagram (2, 3 & 4 Circles)

BEST FOR: helping people see how your framework works together.

HOW TO USE:
→ Place one part of your framework in each circle
→ Use overlaps to show how each affects the other
→ Only works with 2, 3, 4 part frameworks

2️⃣ The Classic Chart

BEST FOR: deep diving every facet of a topic

HOW TO USE:
→ Put each piece of your framework in the columns
→ Compare along different parameters in the rows
→ If the framework has 5 or more parts... flip the axis

3️⃣ The Funnel

BEST FOR: showing how things flow

HOW TO USE:
→ Put each piece of the framework in sequential order
→ Stack them from top to bottom
→ Add boxes/notes outside the funnel to spice it up

4️⃣ The Nested Circles

BEST FOR: showing interrelationship or layers

HOW TO USE:
→ Put the core idea in the middle
→ Build outward with the surrounding layers
→ Good for simplifying a large, complex discipline

5️⃣ The Pyramid

BEST FOR: showing hierarchy

HOW TO USE:
→ Put the foundational idea at the bottom
→ Stack the rest upward by importance or priority
→ May help to put an arrow at the bottom going up

6️⃣ The Decision Tree

BEST FOR: showing multiple paths or outcomes

HOW TO USE:
→ Start with one core question or starting point
→ Branch into different options
→ Keep each branch simple and easy to follow

7️⃣ The Timeline

BEST FOR: showing sequences over time

HOW TO USE:
→ Lay out steps from left to right or top to bottom
→ Add specific timestamps
→ Especially helpful for very practical tasks

8️⃣ The 2x2 Matrix

BEST FOR: simplifying decisions or comparisons

HOW TO USE:
→ Pick two variables for your axes
→ Place each idea in the correct quadrant
→ One quadrant can be best, or all 4 can be equal

NOTE:
Since there are only 8 layouts, in order to stand out you'll have to spice them up.

→ Cool color coding
→ Extra info boxes
→ Combining shapes and charts

But!

Then make it pop.

What is a strong POV?

Essentially, it’s this:

→ A single, industry-level hot take.

It repels the wrong people.
It attracts the right people.

For reference, here are a few POV examples.

My POV is essentially this:

"Founders should aim to build a large audience by turning their expertise into viral content."

→ That is an incredibly attractive idea to some.
→ It is an incredibly repulsive idea to others.

That’s what’s scary about a POV.
It will attract criticism.

But if I didn’t have a POV, I wouldn’t have a business.

A few other POV examples:

→ Josh Lowman: The best companies combine business, product, and brand strategy to create NEW categories.

→ Anthony Pierri & Rob Kaminski: Startup websites should lead with clarity, not vision.

→ Tas Bober: Landing pages should aim to educate, not convert.

→ Will Greenblatt: Aspiring speakers should aim to get paid workshops, not paid keynotes.

For each one of these POVs, there are industry experts who would strongly disagree.

That’s when you know you’re on the right path to something worth repeating.

How do you find your POV?

Here are the six steps:

1️⃣ Identify ICP

→ Write for one specific, real person.
→ Don’t write for “the market.”
→ If you write for everyone, you write for no one.

2️⃣ Choose Anchor Outcome

→ Pick one outcome they deeply want.
→ Don’t stack multiple outcomes to get more buzz.

3️⃣ Identify Misconception

→ Surface one belief that’s holding them back.
→ Make sure people really believe that misconception
→ Don’t just pick a "straw-man" belief

4️⃣ Argue the Alternative

→ Present a better path forward.
→ Don’t hedge it with endless nuance.

5️⃣ Distill to One Sentence

→ Compress your POV into one sharp idea.
→ Contrast the old and the new if possible.
→ Ask if it would make anyone mad. It should.

6️⃣ Repeat It Relentlessly

→ Say it again and again.
→ Don’t reinvent yourself every quarter.

→ the strength of your product
→ your years of experience

It actually depends on where you create on the spectrum.

Here’s what I mean (and how people get this wrong):

Content exists on a spectrum.

→ On one end it's high-level & outcome-oriented
→ On the other it's tactical & action-oriented
→ And everything in between

Roughly 7 layers total.

Here’s what it looks like at a glance.

High Level / Abstract
↑
 | Layer 1 — The outcomes you provide
 | Layer 2 — Your main point of view
 | Layer 3 — Strategic-level content
 | Layer 4 — Framework content
 | Layer 5 — Simple guides
 | Layer 6 — Tactical help
 | Layer 7 — Micro-hacks
↓
Detailed / Practical

Here’s what happens when you roll the content out:

→ The top of the spectrum attracts stakeholders.
→ The bottom of the spectrum attracts practitioners.

→ The top of the spectrum can help close deals.
→ The bottom is what actually grows your audience.

Brilliant people often prefer layers 1, 2 & 3.

→ They think that anything else is "dumbing it down."
→ So they focus there... and their reach stays tiny.

Average thinkers often prefer layers 5, 6 & 7.

→ It feels fun and intuitive to them.
→ So they focus there... and their audience grows.

Yes, you need all 7 layers for a long-term business.

→ Focus on the bottom of the spectrum.

→ Then monetize it as it grows.

"You don't need to have a big following!"
"Just reach the RIGHT people."

There’s some truth to that.

You can sell to people who barely know you.
